entation Training on Listening Comprehension and Affective Outcomes in Arabic as a Foreign Language

Listening comprehension is a fundamental component of second and foreign language acquisition. It enables learners to process spoken input, develop linguistic knowledge, and participate effectively in communicative interactions. Despite its importance, listening remains one of the most challenging skills for learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language (AFL), particularly at the university level, where learners are increasingly exposed to authentic and relatively natural speech.

One major challenge in listening comprehension arises from the continuous nature of spoken language. Unlike written texts, spoken language does not contain explicit visual boundaries between words. Speakers frequently produce words in connected sequences characterized by

, and other phonological processes. Consequently, learners may encounter difficulties identifying familiar lexical items within continuous speech, even when they possess sufficient vocabulary and grammatical knowledge to understand the same material in written form.

However, the ability to exploit these cues efficiently may depend on learners' linguistic experience and familiarity with the phonological characteristics of the target language. Carroll (2004) further argues that learning to perceive words in a second language involves acquiring the relevant perceptual cues for identifying linguistic boundaries in the speech stream.
In Arabic language learning, these challenges may be particularly significant because of the interaction between morphological structure, phonological processes,

Learners may struggle to identify word boundaries in sequences containing attached conjunctions, prepositions, articles, and pronouns, as well as in speech involving assimilation, vowel reduction, and other connected-speech phenomena.

English language classrooms, reported that explicit speech-stream segmentation training improved listening comprehension and linguistic self-confidence. However, the transferability of these findings to university learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language remains insufficiently established. The developmental characteristics, linguistic backgrounds, learning environments, and listening demands of university learners differ considerably from those of primary-school learners.

Furthermore, listening comprehension is not exclusively a cognitive and linguistic process. Against this background, the present study proposes an instructional intervention designed to develop university learners' ability to segment continuous Arabic speech into meaningful linguistic units. It will investigate whether explicit speech-stream segmentation training can improve listening comprehension, reduce listening anxiety, and enhance linguistic self-confidence among learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language.

University learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language frequently experience difficulties understanding spoken Arabic despite having acquired considerable vocabulary and grammatical knowledge. Such difficulties may arise not only from unfamiliar linguistic content but also from learners' limited ability to recognize lexical and syntactic boundaries in continuous speech.

In conventional Arabic language instruction, listening activities often emphasize comprehension of the overall meaning, vocabulary recognition, and answering questions about spoken texts. Although these activities are important, they may not sufficiently address the perceptual processes through which learners identify words and meaningful segments within connected speech.

The absence of explicit instruction in speech-stream segmentation may consequently leave learners dependent on repeated listening, written transcripts, and contextual guessing. These difficulties may increase cognitive demands and contribute to negative emotional experiences during listening tasks, including anxiety, uncertainty, and reduced confidence in their listening abilities.

Although recent research has investigated speech-stream segmentation training in Arabic and English educational contexts, further investigation is required to determine whether this instructional approach is effective for adult university learners studying Arabic as a foreign language.
Therefore, the central problem addressed by this study is the lack of sufficient empirical evidence concerning the effectiveness of explicit speech-stream segmentation training in
improving listening comprehension and affective outcomes among university learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language.
Examine the effect of explicit speech-stream segmentation training on listening comprehension among university learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language.
Investigate the effect of speech-stream segmentation training on learners' listening anxiety.
Examine the effect of speech-stream segmentation training on learners' linguistic self-confidence.
Identify the segmentation strategies employed by learners during listening comprehension tasks.
Explore learners' perceptions of the effectiveness and usefulness of speech-stream segmentation training.
The study seeks to answer the following questions:
To what extent does speech-stream segmentation training improve listening comprehension among university learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language compared with conventional listening instruction?
To what extent does speech-stream segmentation training reduce listening anxiety among university learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language?
To what extent does speech-stream segmentation training enhance linguistic self-confidence among university learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language?
What speech-stream segmentation strategies do learners employ during listening comprehension tasks following the intervention?
How do learners perceive the usefulness of speech-stream segmentation training in developing their Arabic listening abilities?
The following hypotheses will be tested:

University learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language who receive speech-stream segmentation training will demonstrate significantly greater improvement in listening comprehension than learners receiving conventional listening instruction.
University learners who receive speech-stream segmentation training will demonstrate a significantly greater reduction in listening anxiety than learners receiving conventional listening instruction.

University learners who receive speech-stream segmentation training will demonstrate a significantly greater increase in linguistic self-confidence than learners receiving conventional listening instruction.
The study is expected to contribute to Arabic language education in several ways.

The study will extend existing research on speech perception and segmentation by examining its instructional implications for adult learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language. It will contribute to understanding the relationship between perceptual processing of continuous speech, listening comprehension, and affective dimensions of foreign language learning.

The findings may provide Arabic language instructors with practical strategies for teaching learners how to identify meaningful linguistic units in connected speech rather than relying exclusively on vocabulary recognition and comprehension questions.

The study may inform the development of listening curricula that incorporate explicit training in phonological awareness, prosodic perception, lexical boundary recognition, and connected-speech processing.

By investigating listening anxiety and linguistic self-confidence alongside listening comprehension, the study may provide evidence regarding the potential role of perceptually oriented instruction in improving learners' emotional experiences during Arabic listening activities.

The study will contribute to the emerging empirical literature on speech-stream segmentation instruction by examining its application to university-level AFL learners, a population that remains underrepresented in this line of research.
7.1 Speech-Stream Segmentation and Second Language Listening
Speech-stream segmentation refers to the process through which listeners identify and organize continuous acoustic input into meaningful linguistic units, such as words, phrases, and clauses.

Spoken language is characterized by continuity, and acoustic signals do not consistently provide clear boundaries between words. Listeners therefore rely on different sources of information to identify linguistic units and construct meaning.

et al. (2005) proposed a hierarchical framework for speech segmentation in which lexical, segmental, and prosodic cues contribute differently to segmentation. Their findings suggest that listeners integrate multiple cues rather than relying on a single source of information.

Similarly, Sanders and Neville (2000) demonstrated that listeners employ lexical, syntactic, and stress-related information flexibly during speech segmentation. When certain cues are unavailable or unreliable, listeners may increase their reliance on alternative sources of information.

In second language learning, the development of segmentation abilities is particularly important because learners may not possess sufficient experience with the phonological and prosodic patterns of the target language. Carroll (2004) emphasizes that learners must develop the ability to perceive relevant phonetic cues and use them to identify linguistic units within the second-language speech stream.

These findings suggest that speech-stream segmentation is not merely an automatic perceptual process but may also represent a learnable skill that can be developed through explicit instruction and structured practice.
Speech segmentation involves several types of cues that may support learners' identification of meaningful units.
Familiar vocabulary and contextual meaning enable learners to identify known words and infer the boundaries of surrounding linguistic units.
Grammatical structure and knowledge of sentence patterns help learners identify phrase and clause boundaries.
, assimilation, and other phonological characteristics provide information about possible boundaries between linguistic units.
Pauses, pitch movement, duration, rhythm, stress, and
patterns contribute to the identification of meaningful segments in continuous speech.

et al. (2023) investigated the segmentation of continuous speech by first- and second-language speakers of English and highlighted the importance of prosodic and syntactic cues in the segmentation process. Their findings indicate that segmentation strategies are influenced by language experience and by the characteristics of the speech material.
For Arabic learners, instruction that systematically directs attention to these cues may facilitate the identification of words and phrases in connected speech.

(2026) investigated speech-stream segmentation training in primary Arabic and English language classrooms. The findings indicated improvements in listening comprehension and linguistic self-confidence following explicit segmentation instruction.

However, further investigation is necessary to establish the effectiveness of this approach among adult learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language, particularly those whose first languages differ substantially from Arabic in phonological structure and segmentation patterns.

Listening anxiety refers to learners' feelings of tension, apprehension, or discomfort when attempting to understand spoken language. These feelings may arise when learners perceive listening tasks as difficult, unpredictable, or beyond their current linguistic abilities.

Listening self-efficacy refers to learners' beliefs regarding their ability to perform listening-related tasks successfully. It is conceptually related to linguistic self-confidence, although the two constructs should not be treated as identical.
et al. (2020) demonstrated that listening strategy instruction can influence listening comprehension, listening anxiety, and listening self-efficacy among EFL learners.

From an instructional perspective, speech-stream segmentation training may contribute to these affective outcomes by making the listening process more manageable. When learners develop strategies for identifying linguistic boundaries, they may experience greater control over spoken input and become less dependent on repeated listening or immediate access to written transcripts.
Nevertheless, these potential psychological effects require empirical investigation rather than assumption.

The reviewed literature establishes the importance of speech segmentation in spoken language processing and highlights the role of lexical, syntactic, phonological, and prosodic cues in listening comprehension.
Previous research has also explored the relationship between listening strategy instruction, listening anxiety, and self-efficacy.
However, three gaps remain relevant to the present study:
Limited empirical research has specifically investigated speech-stream segmentation training among university learners of Arabic as a Foreign Language.
The pedagogical implications of explicitly teaching segmentation strategies for Arabic connected speech require further systematic investigation.
The relationship between speech-stream segmentation training, listening anxiety, and linguistic self-confidence has not been sufficiently examined within the university-level AFL context.
The present study seeks to address these gaps through a controlled instructional intervention integrating listening comprehension and affective measures.
The study will be informed by three complementary theoretical perspectives.
et al. (2005) proposed that listeners integrate multiple segmentation cues hierarchically. These cues include lexical and structural information, segmental information, and prosodic information.

This framework provides the primary theoretical foundation for designing the segmentation training activities. The intervention will direct learners' attention toward multiple sources of information that may help them identify meaningful units in continuous Arabic speech.

Second language listening involves the interaction of bottom-up processing, through which learners perceive and decode acoustic information, and top-down processing, through which they use linguistic knowledge and contextual expectations to construct meaning.

Speech-stream segmentation training is expected to strengthen the relationship between these processes by helping learners identify linguistic units while simultaneously using lexical, grammatical, and contextual information.
Bandura's (1997) self-efficacy theory provides a conceptual basis for understanding how learners' beliefs about their abilities may influence their engagement, persistence, and performance.
Within the present study, successful experiences in identifying words and meaningful segments in continuous speech may contribute to stronger beliefs in learners' ability to understand spoken Arabic.
Listening anxiety will be examined as a related but distinct affective construct.
The study proposes the following relationship:
A["Speech-Stream Segmentation Training"] --> B["Improved Perceptual Processing"]
A --> C["Increased Awareness of Segmentation Cues"]
The independent variable is speech-stream segmentation training.
Segmentation strategy use and learners' perceptions of the intervention will be examined as supplementary outcomes.

The framework proposes that explicit instruction in segmentation may improve learners' ability to process continuous Arabic speech and may also influence their emotional experiences during listening tasks.
The study will employ a quasi-experimental mixed-methods design involving an experimental group and a comparison group.

Both groups will complete pre-intervention and post-intervention assessments. The experimental group will receive explicit speech-stream segmentation training integrated into listening instruction, whereas the comparison group will receive conventional listening instruction covering the same general topics and linguistic content.
A qualitative component will be incorporated through learner reflections, interviews, or open-ended responses to explore learners' perceptions of the intervention.
The participants will be approximately 60–80 university students enrolled in Arabic as a Foreign Language courses at a university language center or an equivalent educational institution.
Participants will be selected using convenience sampling based on their availability and eligibility for the study.
Where feasible, two comparable intact classes will be assigned to the experimental and comparison conditions.
Be university students learning Arabic as a foreign language.
Have an approximately comparable proficiency level, preferably A2–B1 according to the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR).
Have received sufficient previous instruction in Arabic to recognize basic vocabulary and grammatical structures.
Have no substantial previous formal training in speech-stream segmentation.

The participants' demographic and linguistic backgrounds, including their first languages, duration of Arabic study, and previous exposure to spoken Arabic, will be documented because these factors may influence segmentation performance.
The final sample size will be determined through an a priori statistical power analysis, taking into account the expected effect size, significance level, and desired statistical power.
The study will use the following instruments.
Two equivalent listening comprehension tests will be developed for the pre-test and post-test.
Each test will contain approximately 20 items assessing:
Identification of lexical items in connected speech.
Recognition of relationships between words and phrases.
The audio materials will be appropriate for the participants' proficiency level and will be reviewed by Arabic language teaching specialists.
To minimize test-related learning effects, the pre-test and post-test will use parallel rather than identical forms.
A listening anxiety questionnaire will be adapted from established second-language listening anxiety measures.
The instrument will contain approximately 10–15 items using a five-point Likert scale:
I feel nervous when listening to Arabic spoken at a natural speed.
I become anxious when I cannot identify individual words in spoken Arabic.
I worry that I will misunderstand Arabic speakers.
I feel tense when completing Arabic listening comprehension tasks.
I feel frustrated when I recognize words but cannot understand the whole sentence.
Items will be reviewed to ensure that they measure listening anxiety rather than general foreign language anxiety.
A nine-item questionnaire adapted from the instrument outlined in the preliminary research document will be used to assess learners' linguistic self-confidence.
The items will cover perceived listening competence, willingness to participate, confidence in understanding spoken Arabic, and confidence in engaging with listening activities.
I feel confident when asked to summarize what I have understood in Arabic.
I believe I can participate successfully in Arabic language activities.
I feel prepared to engage in Arabic listening comprehension tasks.
I believe I can understand Arabic topics discussed in class.
I feel comfortable participating in Arabic communication activities.
I believe I can understand spoken Arabic more effectively than before.
I feel confident in my ability to learn Arabic through listening.
I feel more positive about learning Arabic through listening activities.
I believe I can manage Arabic listening tasks even when the speech is unfamiliar.
Responses will be recorded using a five-point Likert scale.
The instrument will be pilot-tested and subjected to reliability and validity procedures before its use in the main study.

The research instruments and intervention materials will be reviewed by at least three experts in Arabic language teaching, second language acquisition, and language assessment.

A pilot study involving approximately 10–15 learners with characteristics similar to the main participants will be conducted to assess the clarity of the instructions, appropriateness of the audio materials, and feasibility of the intervention.

Internal consistency reliability will be examined using Cronbach's alpha or an appropriate alternative. A coefficient of approximately .70 or higher will be considered an initial indicator of acceptable reliability, interpreted alongside the number of items and the construct being measured.
Listening test items will be reviewed for content validity and difficulty. Where appropriate, inter-rater reliability will be calculated for segmentation tasks requiring subjective judgment.
The intervention will consist of six weeks of instruction, with two sessions per week, for a total of 12 sessions.
Each session will last approximately 45 minutes.

The experimental group will receive explicit instruction and guided practice in speech-stream segmentation, while the comparison group will receive conventional listening instruction using comparable audio materials and topics.
The training will be based on the following instructional principles:
Gradual progression from shorter to longer speech segments.
Explicit attention to phonological and prosodic cues.
Integration of listening, vocabulary, and grammatical knowledge.
Guided practice followed by independent listening.
Gradual reduction of reliance on written transcripts.

Potential themes may include increased awareness of connected speech, perceived improvement in listening ability, changes in listening strategies, reduced anxiety, and greater confidence. These will be treated as possible themes rather than predetermined findings.
Quantitative and qualitative results will be integrated during interpretation.
For example, changes in listening comprehension scores may be examined alongside learners' reflections concerning the strategies they found most useful.
This integration will help explain not only whether the intervention is effective but also how learners perceive and experience the instructional process.
The study will comply with institutional research ethics requirements.
The following measures will be implemented:
Participants will receive clear information about the study and its procedures.
Participants will be informed of their right to withdraw without penalty.
Data will be securely stored and used exclusively for research purposes.
The instructional intervention will not negatively affect participants' course grades.
Both groups will receive appropriate listening instruction.
The comparison group may be offered access to the segmentation training materials after the study.
Based on the theoretical framework and previous research, the study anticipates that explicit speech-stream segmentation training may produce improvements in learners' listening comprehension.
It is also anticipated that learners who receive segmentation training may report lower listening anxiety and higher linguistic self-confidence than learners receiving conventional instruction.
The study may further reveal that learners become more aware of the role of phonological, prosodic, lexical, and syntactic cues in understanding continuous Arabic speech.
However, these expectations remain hypotheses. The actual findings will depend on the participants, instructional materials, intervention implementation, and statistical results.
Several limitations may affect the interpretation of the findings.
First, the study will be conducted within a single university or language-learning context, which may limit the generalizability of the results.
Second, the use of intact classes and convenience sampling may introduce selection-related differences between groups.
Third, learners' first languages may influence their segmentation strategies and perception of Arabic connected speech.
Fourth, the six-week intervention may be insufficient to establish whether improvements in segmentation and listening comprehension are maintained over time.
Fifth, listening anxiety and linguistic self-confidence will be measured primarily through self-report questionnaires, which may be influenced by learners' perceptions and response tendencies.

Finally, the study will focus on Modern Standard Arabic at a specified proficiency level. Its findings may not automatically generalize to learners of Arabic dialects or learners at substantially different proficiency levels.
This proposed study aims to investigate the pedagogical potential of speech-stream segmentation training in university-level Arabic as a Foreign Language instruction.

By integrating listening comprehension, listening anxiety, and linguistic self-confidence into a single research design, the study seeks to extend existing research on speech perception and segmentation into a foreign language educational context.

The proposed intervention will provide explicit and systematic training in identifying meaningful units in continuous Arabic speech through the use of phonological, prosodic, lexical, and syntactic cues.

The findings may contribute to the development of evidence-based listening instruction and offer practical insights into the design of Arabic listening curricula that address both the cognitive and affective dimensions of language learning.

Ultimately, the study aims to establish whether teaching learners how to segment continuous speech can provide a valuable complement to conventional listening instruction and support the development of more effective and confident Arabic language learners.
